description: Excalidraw's 39-second launch video for the Excalidraw CLI, which renders Excalidraw diagrams from Excalidraw+ or local files so AI agents can see and check their own diagrams. The video pairs a hand-drawn title ('Render any scene to PNG') with a clean terminal session listing and rendering scenes. It's a strong reference for a short, focused developer-tool intro: one capability, shown in the product's own visual language, ending on a one-line call to action ('Install today').
text:
Excalidraw CLI released!

Log in to your Excalidraw+ account or use with local files.

You can easily render Excalidraw diagrams to give better output feedback to your agents.

Install today.
replies_summary: Overwhelmingly positive and practical: most replies latch onto the agent 'render loop' — letting agents render and look at their own diagrams so humans can spot misunderstandings fast — and several users report already adding it to workflows. Recurring questions are about pricing ('Is it free to use?'), CLI vs. MCP, and whether the rendered PNG flows back into the agent's context; a few push long-standing feature requests (subfolders) or name alternatives (tldraw, Mermaid). Quote posts echo the same theme ('My agents will love this') across English, Japanese, Turkish, Portuguese, Chinese and Korean audiences.

notable_replies.text: A CLI for diagrams is sneaky useful: agents can render what they think the system looks like, and humans can spot the misunderstanding in seconds.
letting agents render and look at their own output is so underrated.
Tried it. Great work, adding it to my daily workflows.
But what about a simple feature like subfolders? It’s been pending for years 😅

notable_replies.text: Tagged as AI generated on TikTok, new model? 👀 https://t.co/cLcLAm1GZv
F, my kid can draw better than that

notable_replies.text: Wait, yoooooo, this font-variation-setting is actually so friggin' cute ♡ https://t.co/cQQvVxHnzm

description: A short 6-second explainer for OpenAI Private Intelligence that animates a clean diagram of customer and OpenAI environments, with labeled boundaries for data access, tools, permitted actions and approvals. A good reference for turning a security architecture into a calm, legible system diagram.
text:
Privacy should advance as fast as intelligence. OpenAI Private Intelligence gives businesses stronger controls over their data while using our most capable models.

We’re building these protections in close collaboration with some of our largest customers to help businesses apply frontier AI to their most sensitive work.
https://t.co/BiA4N8FQVH
replies_summary: Replies are skeptical and enterprise-minded: people ask how the privacy can be verified, whether data processing or just access changes, and what retention and auditability look like. Several call it a promise without pricing, timeline or named customers.

notable_replies.text: how do we verify that it’s actually private?
Controls over what a model can access are a good step. The next question is retention. The safest data is the data that was never stored.

OpenAI promises businesses stronger data controls and calls it Private Intelligence. No pricing, no timeline, no named customers. A promise is not a product, and on the floor you count the locks, not the slogans.

description: Emil Kowalski demos a 244-term vocabulary inside his course site, where terms get a dotted underline and you can hover for a definition or click for a live animation demo. An excellent reference for inline, interactive glossary patterns on an educational website.
text:
Using the right words can drastically improve the results you get from your agents, which is why I built a vocabulary of 244 terms for https://t.co/ItfxHzSjMc.

If a term is used in a lesson, it gets a dotted underline. You can hover to see its definition or click to see a demo. https://t.co/KSxYQpH9mJ
replies_summary: Replies praise pairing each definition with a live demo, saying seeing the behavior teaches the judgment to ask for it. Others ask for reverse browsing from demos to terms or a side-by-side of vague versus precise prompts, and several lament the course price.

notable_replies.text: The demo beside the definition is what makes this teachable. A learner can see the behavior, learn its name, then describe it precisely next time instead of trying variations of “make it feel better.”
The click-through demo is the important bit. A definition gives you the word; seeing the behaviour gives you the judgment to know when to ask for it.

Can you browse from the demos back to the terms?
Sometimes you know what you want it to do, just not what to call it.

description: A 10-second screen capture of the Local LLM iOS app, where the on-device LFM3 1.7B model builds a small interactive webpage right on an iPhone, framed with a simple headline and "Available in Local LLM" caption. A neat reference for a short, proof-by-demo app announcement.

A small interactive webpage, made locally on iPhone.

https://t.co/odh8xMF2ab

notable_replies.text: A tiny model making something you can actually tap and play with is a much more fun demo than another wall of benchmark scores.
A 1.7B model building a webpage on-device is a nice demo. How much memory does it use while generating? That's usually the limit on older iPhones.
On this screen you should add the thing you have in your Dynamic Island version where it shows how much data has already been downloaded https://t.co/Wwj9cUttUH

description: A 68-second product demo from Zed announcing multiplayer Claude Code via DeltaDB, showing a terminal session shared between teammates on a clean light canvas. A solid reference for demoing an invisible collaboration feature with simple, focused screen recording.
text:

Run `/delta share` in Claude Code, and your teammate joins in their own session with your full context and uncommitted work. You're both working on the same thread, backed by DeltaDB.

https://t.co/prGSZiSzHm https://t.co/4ceGfMA1qk
replies_summary: Replies are split: some like sharing uncommitted work with full context and ask how simultaneous edits to the same file work, while others say they don't understand the use case for multiplayer AI. A couple report setup problems and timeouts.

notable_replies.text: Sharing uncommitted work with full context is the bit I'd use most. Handing off a half-done branch usually means writing a long note nobody reads.
I'm a huge fan of Zed. I do not understand multiplayer AI at all.
Sharing uncommitted work in the session is the useful part. Curious how it handles two people editing the same file at the same moment.

description: A 67-second live-action launch film for Sentient OS (YC F26), an on-device AI that learns your life overnight with a local LLM, shot outdoors in a park rather than on a screen. A useful reference for grounding a technical app launch in everyday, human footage.
text: Today, we're launching Sentient OS (YC F26), on-device AI that understands your life overnight with a local LLM. This unlimited inference enables 2 magical experiences 🧵 https://t.co/SFFAAnrxdj
replies_summary: Replies are mostly congratulations plus thoughtful product questions: praise for the local-first, overnight approach and the local markdown files, alongside questions about day-two retention, correcting wrong memories, and why setup asks for a ChatGPT subscription despite being on-device.

notable_replies.text: local markdown files is actually the smartest design choice here
Letting a local model do the heavy thinking overnight, so nothing leaves the Mac, is a smart way to make on-device AI feel generous instead of limited. Congrats on the launch.
The harder part is the habit. What does it do on day one that makes someone open it again on day two?

description: A 12-second square launch loop for AfterQuery Data Partnerships: a serif headline ("Your company's data, licensed with care.") over a soft pastel gradient with animated vertical barcode-like lines. A tidy reference for a calm, typographic B2B announcement that fits in one glance.
text:
Frontier models nearly run through the public internet for pre-training alone. The knowledge they need next is locked inside businesses.

Today we're launching @AfterQuery Data Partnerships.

If you're a business owner who is curious, or hesitant, about licensing your data, we would love to hear from you.

Learn more in the replies.
replies_summary: Replies focus on the business idea rather than the visual: people agree the next useful training data sits inside companies, but note that cleanup, permissions and stripping PII are the hard part. Several replies are data vendors pitching their own services.

notable_replies.text: The next wave of useful training data really does sit inside companies rather than on the public web. The hard part will be the cleanup and permissions work, which usually takes longer than the actual deal.

The public web was the easy training set.
The next gains live inside private business data.
Licensing with care is what makes that data usable.
most of what a small firm knows sits in email threads with client names in them. licensing starts with who strips those out.

description: Obsidian 1.15 early-access release video covering faster themed Mermaid diagrams, Lock Screen voice capture on iOS and more. A good reference for presenting a multi-feature release as a short video with a scannable changelog caption.
text:
Obsidian 1.15.0 (early access) is now available to Catalyst members!

- Mermaid diagrams use our new rendering engine, Pele, which renders up to 500 times faster and uses your theme's colors and fonts.
- Voice capture on iOS: Quick Capture can record and transcribe voice notes as you speak, even from the Lock Screen.
- PDF export on mobile.
- Smarter list editing: indenting or moving a list item now moves nested items too.
- Accent-insensitive search: cafe matches café in suggestions.
- New URI and CLI commands to append or prepend content under a heading.
- Filters in Bases can now be reordered.
- Community plugins load faster when Obsidian starts.
replies_summary: Replies are enthusiastic about voice capture and accent-insensitive search, with Android users asking when features arrive there and others asking technical questions about the new Pele renderer and how the 500x speedup was measured.

notable_replies.text: Accent insensitive search!!! ty! After waiting for years I finally decided to build a plugin two weeks ago. If only I’d known, I would have waited.

description: GitHub's product film for the Logitech MX Keypad integrated with the GitHub Copilot app, showing physical keys mapped to agent prompts and sessions. A reference for a hardware-meets-software intro that sells a workflow rather than specs.

description: Supabase announces running Supabase locally without Docker, plus a separate local project per coding agent. Reference for a developer-launch video that leads with a long-requested pain point.

description: Emil Kowalski on a motion-design principle for UI: bigger elements (and longer distances) should animate more slowly because they feel heavier, illustrated with a hand vs. cursors animation. Reference for animation timing on websites and interfaces.
text:
The bigger an animated element is, the slower it should move.

Notice how the hand on the right moves much slower than the cursors on the left. That’s because it feels heavier.

The same applies to distance. The more an element has to travel, the longer the animation should be. https://t.co/lFDygrDF4u
replies_summary: Strong agreement that matching mass/distance to duration is what makes motion 'feel right'. Commenters extend it to static spacing and ask whether to scale duration linearly; motion-school folks note it's a classic principle.

notable_replies.text: Works for static layouts too. The bigger the element, the more room it needs around it.  Same physics, just frozen.
this is the kind of detail that separates "works" from "feels right".
E=mc²

description: Warp introduces Warp Factories, 'Terraform for agents': one repository that configures agents, automations, access/environments and measurement as code. A very high-reach (~955K impressions) reference for explaining an abstract platform concept with an analogy plus a demo video.
text:
Agents are getting complex to manage: models, skills, automations, permissions, cloud environments, orchestration patterns...

So, we built the Terraform for agents: one repository that configures all of your agents as code.

The Warp Factories configuration spec defines:
- Agents and orchestration: how work gets routed and which models agents use
- Automations: the events and schedules that kick off work
- Access and environments: repositories, secrets, MCP servers, and runners
- Measurement: scorers and benchmarks for understanding and improving performance

Because it’s all code, both engineers and agents can propose changes to the factory itself. That makes it possible to test new configurations, benchmark them, and even have your factory propose improvements as PRs.
replies_summary: Engaged and mostly constructive: replies agree that managing agents is becoming its own discipline and that agents-as-code is the right shape. They raise version pinning, permissions and revoke paths, with some irony about writing YAML to manage AI.

notable_replies.text: we've come full circle: AI was supposed to delete YAML. now we're writing YAML to manage the AI.
